source_text: Οὐ γὰρ μωραίνομεν, ἄνδρες Ἕλληνες, οὐδὲ λήρους ἀπαγγέλλομεν, θεὸν ἐν ἀνθρώπου μορφῇ γεγονέναι καταγγέλλοντες. Οἱ λοιδοροῦντες ἡμᾶς συγκρίνατε τοὺς μύθους ὑμῶν τοῖς ἡμετέροις διηγήμασι. Δηΐφοβος, ὥς φασιν, ἦν ἡ Ἀθηνᾶ διὰ τὸν Ἕκτορα, καὶ χάριν Ἀδμήτου Φοῖβος ἀκειρεκόμης τὰς εἰλίποδας βοῦς ἐποίμαινε, καὶ πρεσβύτις ἀφικνεῖται πρὸς τὴν Σεμέλην ἡ τοῦ Διὸς γαμετή.Τοιαῦτα δὲ μελετῶντες πῶς ἡμᾶς διαγελᾶτε; Τέθνηκεν ὑμῶν ὁ Ἀσκληπιός, καὶ ὁ τὰς πεντήκοντα παρθένους μιᾷ νυκτὶ Θεσπιάσι διακορεύσας βορᾷ πυρὸς ἑαυτὸν παραδοὺς οἴχεται. Προμηθεὺς τῷ Καυκάσῳ προσαρτηθεὶς τιμωρίαν χάριν τῆς εἰς ἀνθρώπους εὐεργεσίας ὑπήνεγκεν. Φθονερὸς ὁ Ζεὺς καθ᾿ ὑμᾶς, καὶ κρύπτει τὸν ὄνειρον τοῖς ἀνθρώποις βουλόμενος ἀπόλλυσθαι. Διόπερ ἀποβλέψαντες πρὸς τὰ οἰκεῖα ἀπομνημονεύματα κἄν ὡς ὁμοίως μυθολογοῦντας ἀποδέξασθε. Καὶ ἡμεῖς μὲν οὐκ ἀφραίνομεν, φλήναφα δὲ τὰ ὑμέτερα. Γένεσιν ἄν λέγητε θεῶν, καὶ θνητοὺς αὐτοὺς ἀποφανεῖσθε. Διὰ τί γὰρ οὐ κύει νῦν ἡ Ἥρα; Πότερον γεγήρακεν, ἤ τοῦ μηνύσαντος ὑμῖν ἀπορεῖται; Πείσθητέ μοι νῦν, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἕλληνες, μηδὲ τοὺς μύθους μηδὲ τοὺς θεοὺς ὑμῶν ἀλληγορήσητε. Κἄν γὰρ τοῦτο πράττειν ἐπιχειρήσητε, θεότης ἡ καθ᾿ ὑμᾶς ἀνῄρηται καὶ ὑφ᾿ ὑμῶν· οἱ γὰρ τοιοῦτοι παρ᾿ ὑμῖν ὄντες οἱ δαίμονες, ὁποῖοι καὶ λέγονται, φαῦλοι τὸν τρόπον εἰσίν, ἢ μεταγενόμενοι πρὸς τὸ φυσικώτερον οὔκ εἰσιν οἷοι καὶ λέγονται. Σέβειν δὲ τῶν στοιχείων τὴν ὑπόστασιν οὔτ᾿ ἂν πεισθείην, οὔτ᾿ ἂν πείσαιμι τὸν πλησίον.Καὶ Μητρόδωρος δὲ ὁ Λαμψακηνὸς ἐν τῷ περὶ Ὁμήρου λίαν εὐήθως διείλεκται, πάντα εἰς ἀλληγορίαν μετάγων. Οὔτε γὰρ Ἥραν οὔτε Ἀθηνᾶν οὔτε Δία τοῦτ᾿ εἶναί φησιν ὅπερ οἱ τοὺς περιβόλους αὐτοῖς καὶ τεμένη καθιδρύσαντες νομίζουσι, φύσεως δὲ ὑποστάσεις καὶ στοιχείων διακοσμήσεις. Καὶ τὸν Ἕκτορα δὲ καὶ τὸν Ἀχιλλέα δηλαδὴ καὶ τὸν Ἀγαμέμνονα καὶ πάντας ἁπαξαπλῶς Ἕλληνάς τε καὶ βαρβάρους σὺν τῇ Ἑλένῃ καὶ τῷ Πάριδι, τῆς αὐτῆς φύσεως ὑπάρχοντας, χάριν οἰκονομίας ἐρεῖτε παρεισῆχθαι, οὐδενὸς ὄντος τῶν προειρημένων ἀνθρώπων. Ταῦτα δὲ ἡμεῖς προετείναμεν ὥσπερ ἐπὶ ὑποθέσεως· τὴν γὰρ ἡμετέραν περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ κατάληψιν οὐδὲ συγκρίνειν ὅσιον τοῖς εἰς ὕλην καὶ βόρβορον κυλινδουμένοις.
pass_a_gloss: For we do not speak foolishly, men Greeks, nor do we announce empty words, announcing God to have come in human form. You who revile us, compare your myths to our stories. Deiphobus, as they say, was Athena on account of Hector, and Phoebus, unmutilated, pastured the crippled oxen for the sake of Admetus, and an old woman arrives at Semele, the wife of Zeus. And practicing such things, how do you laugh at us? Your Asclepius died, and the one who corrupted the fifty virgins of the Thespians in one night, having devoured himself with fire, departs. Prometheus, having been bound to the Caucasus, endured punishment for the benefit he conferred on men. Zeus is envious towards you, and hides the dream from men, wishing them to perish. Therefore, looking at your own memories, even if you accept us as speaking similarly in myths. And we do not speak foolishly, but we despise your things. You might say the birth of gods, and you will declare them to be mortal. Why does Hera not conceive now? Has she grown old, or is she at a loss because the one who announced it to you? Be persuaded by me now, men Greeks, and do not allegorize your myths or your gods. For even if you attempt to do this, the divinity according to you is destroyed and by you; for the such-like beings among you, who are called demons, are of a worthless character, or having come later, they are not as they are said to be, towards what is more natural. And I would not be persuaded to reverence the substance of the elements, nor would I persuade the one next to me. And Metrodorus of Lampsacus also, in his work on Homer, has spoken very piously, transferring everything to allegory. For he says that neither Hera nor Athena nor Zeus is what those who have built temples and precincts around them think, but rather substances of nature and adornments of elements. And he will say that Hector and Achilles and Agamemnon and all the Greeks and barbarians, along with Helen and Paris, being of the same nature, were introduced for the sake of economy, none of the aforementioned people being real. But we have proposed these things as if on a hypothesis; for it is not holy to compare our understanding of God to those who are rolled in matter and mud.
pass_b_english: We do not speak foolishly, Greeks, nor do we proclaim empty tales when we announce that God has come in human form. You who revile us, compare your myths to our accounts. They say Deiphobus was Athena because of Hector, and Phoebus, with his unshorn hair, tended Admetus's crippled oxen as a favor, and an old woman came to Semele, the wife of Zeus. Practicing such stories, how do you mock us? Your Asclepius died, and the man who deflowered the fifty Thespian virgins in a single night, after consuming himself with fire, is gone. Prometheus, bound to the Caucasus, suffered punishment for the benefit he gave to humanity. Zeus is envious toward you and hides the dream from mankind, wishing them to perish. So look to your own records and, even if you accept us as merely spinning similar myths, you will see the difference. We are not foolish; we despise your inventions. You may claim a birth for the gods, yet you declare them mortal. Why does Hera not conceive now? Has she grown old, or is she at a loss because the one who announced it to you has failed? Be persuaded now, Greeks, and do not allegorize either your myths or your gods. For even if you attempt this, the divinity you worship is annulled by your own doing; the beings you call demons are base in character, or, having arisen later, they are not what they are said to be in any more natural sense. I would not be persuaded to reverence the substance of the elements, nor would I persuade anyone else to do so. Metrodorus of Lampsacus, in his work on Homer, has spoken with excessive credulity, turning everything into allegory. He claims that neither Hera nor Athena nor Zeus is what those who built them temples and shrines suppose, but rather manifestations of nature and adornments of the elements. He will also say that Hector, Achilles, Agamemnon, all Greeks and barbarians alike, along with Helen and Paris—since they share the same nature—were introduced for the sake of poetic economy, none of those named individuals having actually existed. We have proposed these points only hypothetically, for it is not right even to compare our understanding of God with those who are rolled about in matter and mud.

review.notes: Pass A fails on several counts of accuracy and completeness compared to the Greek. 1. Inaccuracy: 'unmutilated' for 'ἀκειρεκόμης' (unshorn/not cut) is a poor choice in this context, though Pass B corrects it. 2. Inaccuracy/Omission: 'the one who announced it to you' for 'τοῦ μηνύσαντος ὑμῖν' is an incomplete rendering of the Greek clause; the Greek implies the one who announced/signaled, but Pass A's English structure 'or is she at a loss because the one who announced it to you?' is ungrammatical and fails to capture the sense of the Greek question. 3. Inaccuracy: 'the divinity according to you is destroyed and by you' for 'θεότης ἡ καθ᾿ ὑμᾶς ἀνῄρηται καὶ ὑφ᾿ ὑμῶν' is a clumsy translation of 'the divinity [which is] held up/exalted according to you and by you'. 4. Inaccuracy: 'the such-like beings' for 'οἱ τοιοῦτοι' is awkward. 5. Inaccuracy: 'the one next to me' for 'τὸν πλησίον' (the neighbor/one near me) is acceptable but Pass A's 'nor would I persuade the one next to me' misses the nuance of 'nor would I be persuaded to... nor would I persuade'. Most importantly, Pass A fails to translate 'εὐήθως' (piously/willingly/readily) in the context of Metrodorus, translating it as 'very piously' while the Greek 'εὐήθως' in this context often carries a sense of 'readily' or 'willingly' (often used sarcastically or to mean 'with ease'), and Pass B's 'with excessive credulity' is a better interpretive choice, but Pass A's 'very piously' is a weak rendering of the specific adverbial sense here. However, the primary failure is the grammatical collapse in the Hera clause: 'or is she at a loss because the one who announced it to you?' which lacks a predicate/verb to complete the thought presented in the Greek.
